title: Unions & Collective Bargaining
narrativeQuestion: How did workers try to turn individual vulnerability into collective power, and why did one national labor model collapse while another endured?

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.claim: Nine Philadelphia garment cutters formed the Knights of Labor in 1869 from a position of weakness and secrecy.

chapters.title: Collective power
chapters.claim: A worker who can be replaced alone may gain leverage when enough workers can stop the system together.

chapters.title: Nothing protected them
chapters.claim: Late nineteenth-century workers lacked the federal organizing and bargaining protections that would come decades later.

chapters.title: Terence V. Powderly
chapters.claim: Powderly led the Knights during their rise while favoring broad reform and often approaching strikes cautiously.

chapters.title: Who was in, and who was out
chapters.claim: The Knights organized unusually broadly for their era, including many women and Black workers, while equality remained inconsistent and important exclusions persisted.

chapters.title: What they actually wanted
chapters.claim: The Knights imagined education, mutual aid, and cooperation as alternatives to dependence on wages alone.

chapters.title: They beat Jay Gould
chapters.claim: The 1885 Wabash strike showed that coordinated workers could force a powerful railroad system to stop and negotiate.

namedPeople.name: Jay Gould
namedPeople.anchorNote: Verified public-domain Library of Congress photograph, tonally graded and credited on the page as an archival photograph.

chapters.title: 110,000 to 720,000
chapters.claim: Victory helped drive explosive growth, but rapid expansion also created organizational strain.

chapters.title: One firing becomes a five-state strike
chapters.claim: The firing of C. A. Hall in Marshall, Texas became a trigger in a much larger railroad conflict.

chapters.title: The train moves again
chapters.claim: The Great Southwest Railroad Strike failed as trains kept moving under replacement labor, legal pressure, and armed enforcement.

chapters.title: Haymarket backlash
chapters.claim: The Knights did not organize the Haymarket meeting, but public backlash damaged organized labor broadly and intensified the Knights' decline.

chapters.title: The other model
chapters.claim: The AFL's narrower craft-federation model made different trade-offs and proved more institutionally durable.

namedPeople.name: Samuel Gompers
namedPeople.anchorNote: Verified public-domain Library of Congress photograph, c1902 during his AFL presidency rather than at the 1886 founding; the page states the date.

chapters.title: The words for what you saw
chapters.claim: Labor vocabulary becomes easier to retain when attached to conflicts and choices students have already experienced.

chapters.title: Note repair
chapters.claim: The ending compresses the narrative into a corrected, readable reference students can use after the experience.

accuracyNotes: Use nine Philadelphia garment cutters for the December 1869 founding group.
Describe the Knights as a broad national labor organization with mixed assemblies rather than equating them mechanically with later CIO industrial unionism.

Women and Black workers participated in substantial numbers, but local segregation, inconsistent enforcement, anti-Chinese politics, and occupational exclusions complicate any simple inclusiveness claim.
C. A. Hall was fired after attending a Knights meeting on company time according to major historical accounts; the union regarded the firing as violating the 1885 agreement.
Do not imply that violating every labor injunction automatically produced jail without a jury; explain judicial contempt power more carefully.
The standalone AFL existed from 1886 until the 1955 AFL-CIO merger; describe durability as institutional/model continuity, not an unchanged century-long organization.

Named-person visual anchors: Powderly is a source-derived stylization and is labelled as such; Gould and Gompers are unaltered Library of Congress photographs under a tonal grade and are credited as archival photographs; C. A. Hall is an interpretive reconstruction and must never be presented as a likeness.
